title-group.article-title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects of intravenous dexamethasone on postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty

sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: Dexamethasone has shown promising efficacy in alleviating pain and enhancing outcomes undergoing TKA. However, an optimal route of administration, dosage, and treatment duration have not yet been established. This study is to assess the effects of intravenous dexamethasone administration on postoperative pain management and prognosis in patients undergoing TKA.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Data were retrieved from PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science to compare the effects of intravenous dexamethasone administration versus non-administration on outcomes following TKA. Primary endpoints included pain scores and morphine consumption. Secondary endpoints comprised walking distance, ROM, patients requiring rescue analgesics and antiemetics, LOS, levels of CRP and IL-6, QoR, and the incidence of adverse events.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: This meta-analysis included 15 RCTs involving 2,584 patients. The study indicated that intravenous dexamethasone can decrease VAS scores at rest (24 h, 95% CI: -0.71 [-0.86, -0.55], I²=66%, P < 0.00001; 48 h, 95% CI: -0.30 [-0.43, -0.18], I²=46%, P < 0.00001) and movement (24 h, 95% CI: -0.89 [-1.23, -0.55], I²=91%,P < 0.00001; 48 h, 95% CI: -0.42 [-0.62, -0.23], I²=84%, P < 0.0001). Moreover, it can reduce morphine consumption (24 h, 95% CI: -3.06 [-4.82, -1.30], I²=46%, P = 0.0006; 48 h, 95% CI: -5.23 [-8.28, -2.18], I²=76%, P = 0.0008) and increase walking distances on postoperative days 1 to 3, and improve the ROM on postoperative day 1 to 2. Furthermore, intravenous dexamethasone reduced the need for requiring rescue analgesics and antiemetics, shortened LOS, lowered CRP and IL-6 levels, and improved the quality of life after TKA. The incidence of infection, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, wound healing, or deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism did not differ significantly. Subgroup analyses revealed no significant differences between single-administration and repeat-administration groups, except in the context of rescue antiemetic requirements.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our study revealed that a single intravenous dose of dexamethasone, ranging from 8 to 16 mg administered before or after the induction of anesthesia or one hour prior to surgery, is efficacious in diminishing postoperative pain and cumulative morphine consumption, reducing the necessity for rescue analgesics and antiemetics, and shorten LOS for TKA. Additionally, it contributed to an increase in postoperative walking distance, ROM, and overall quality of postoperative recovery.

sec.title: Trial registration
sec.p: We conducted literature selection, eligibility criteria evaluation, data extraction and analysis on the research program registered in Prospero (CRD42024521224) in January 2025.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) represents a main therapeutic strategy for addressing end-stage knee osteoarthritis and other knee-related disorders, markedly enhancing postoperative pain management and functional recovery, thereby improving the quality of life of patient [1]. Over the past decade, there has been a progressive increase in the number of individuals undergoing TKA, with projections indicating that the annual TKA procedures in the United States may ascend to 3.5 million by 2030 [2]. Consequently, TKA has evolved into a conventional operation within the field of orthopedics. However, post-TKA pain remains a significant challenge, affecting both patients and healthcare providers. Issues such as increased opioid usage, reduced walking capabilities and range of motion(ROM), prolonged length of stay(LOS), and the risk of deep vein thrombosis detrimentally impact patient satisfaction [3]. Despite advancements in perioperative pain management strategies and the adoption of multimodal analgesic approaches in TKA [4], leading to the potential realization of pain-free wards’, the lack of standardized guidelines regarding the selection, dosage, frequency, and administration method for multimodal analgesia underscores the ongoing need for effective postoperative pain management strategies.

Glucocorticoids, primarily cortisol, are steroid hormones produced by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex, playing a critical role in the regulation of the biosynthesis and metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, while also exhibiting potent analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antiemetic properties [5]. Dexamethasone, in particular, has been extensively utilized for its effectiveness in mitigating postoperative nausea and vomiting and reducing postoperative pain, thereby facilitating an expedited postoperative recovery [6–8]. A recent guideline has advocated for the intravenous administration of 8–10 mg dexamethasone during total hip arthroplasty to leverage its analgesic and antiemetic benefits [9]. However, despite the publication of several meta-analyses on the application of dexamethasone in TKA [10–13], definitive recommendations regarding its optimal use remain elusive, with the inclusion of case-control studies, varying administration routes, and combined analysis with total hip arthroplasty studies detracting from the reliability of these findings.

To date, only one meta-analysis exclusively investigating the correlation between perioperative dexamethasone administration and post-TKA pain relief, encompassing all randomized controlled trials, has been documented [14]. With the recent publication of additional randomized controlled trials focusing on intravenous dexamethasone and post-TKA pain within the past two years, there has been a significant increase in both the patient sample size and the introduction of novel outcome measures. Hence, our study aims to conduct a more inclusive systematic review and meta-analysis, integrating recent randomized controlled trials to enrich the existing evidence base. This approach will enable a more accurate determination of the optimal administration route, dosage, and treatment duration of intravenous dexamethasone for improving postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty.

sec.title: Data and literature sources
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in strict accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [15]. This work was carried out according to a predefined protocol that was registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD42024521224) prior to the review. Comprehensive literature searches were performed in PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science up to January 2025, without imposing language or time limitations. The search strategy utilized MeSH terms including “Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee” and “Dexamethasone.” Detailed search methodologies are documented in Annex 1. Additionally, references from included studies and previous meta-analyses were meticulously reviewed for pertinent studies.

sec.title: Inclusion criteria
sec.p: Eligibility for inclusion was granted to all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) adhering to the following specifications: (1) studies involving adult patients undergoing unilateral TKA only, (2) the experimental group received intravenous dexamethasone alone while the control group was administered an equivalent dose of placebo or saline; if dexamethasone was combined with another drug, the control had to receive the same drug in an identical dosage and route, and (3) reported outcomes included at least one of the following: pain scores, cumulative morphine consumption, the necessity for rescue analgesics or antiemetics, LOS, walking distance, ROM, muscle power scale, or specific adverse events linked to dexamethasone such as infections, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, issues with wound healing, and thromboembolic events.

sec.title: Exclusion criteria
sec.p:
Studies were excluded if they (1) failed to meet the inclusion standards, (2) were RCTs or non-human trials lacking accessible data. Additionally, three studies were omitted due to retraction related to academic integrity concerns [16–18]. Article selection was independently conducted by two authors from the aforementioned databases, following the established strategy, with any differences resolved by a third reviewer. The screening process is illustrated in Fig. 1.Fig. 1
PRISMA flow diagram of the identification and selection of the studies included in this meta-analysis

sec.title: Data extraction and analysis
sec.p: Data extracted included: first author, publication year, patient ages and numbers, anesthesia type, dexamethasone dosage and its comparator, duration of administration, follow-up length, and primary outcomes such as postoperative pain scores (utilizing visual analog scale (VAS) or numerical rating scale (NRS)), cumulative morphine consumption, LOS, and noted adverse events. Pain scores recorded on the 0–100 mm VAS were translated into 11-point VAS scores for consistency. Two reviewers independently extracted data from figures and tables, resolving any discrepancies through consultation with a third reviewer.

sec.title: Quality of evidence and risk of bias assessment
sec.p:
The quality of evidence and risk of bias for all RCTs was assessed for methodological quality by two researchers using the Cochrane Collaboration’s risk of bias tool. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion by a third researcher. Risk of bias was classified as low, high or unclear, with green circles indicating low risk of bias; red circles representing high risk of bias; and yellow circles indicating unclear risk of bias. RCTs were considered to be high quality literature, however, the level of evidence may be reduced due to risk of bias, heterogeneity, imprecision and publication bias. Of these, seven studies were at low risk of bias, six were at unclear risk of bias, and two were at high risk of bias (Fig. 2).Fig. 2
Risk of bias summary. Green color low risk of bias., Yellow color unclear risk of bias, Red color high risk of bias

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.3 (Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, Denmark) and Stata16 (Stata Corp, College Station, TX, USA). Following the approach of McGrath et al. [19], median value and interquartile ranges (IQRs) for continuous variables were converted to mean ± standard deviation (SD) for inclusion in statistical analyses. We calculated the weighted mean difference (WMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for continuous variables, and relative risk or risk difference (RR or RD) with 95% CIs for dichotomous variables. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Study heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, categorizing I² values below 50%, between 50% and 75%, and above 75% as indicative of low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. Due to anticipated clinical variability among the studies, a random-effects model was adopted as the default for estimating combined effect sizes. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots when more than ten studies were included. Subgroup analyses were performed based on dexamethasone dosage (single vs. repeated doses), with significant subgroup interaction (P < 0.05) indicating a differential intervention effect warranting additional discussion, as per Cochrane Handbook guidelines [20].

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Table 1 summarizes the characteristics of 15 RCTs, encompassing a total of 2,584 patients [21–35]. The administered single doses of dexamethasone varied between 8 and 24 mg, with the most common dosage being 10 mg. Nine of these RCTs [22, 23, 26, 28, 31–35] implemented repeated dexamethasone dosing. Anesthesia types varied across studies, including general anesthesia(GA) in six to seven trials [23, 26, 28, 31–34], spinal anesthesia(SA) in six to seven trials [21–24, 29, 30, 35], one instance of SA combined with continuous femoral nerve block(cFNB) [25], and one trial utilizing epidural anesthesia(EA) [27]. The duration of perioperative pain management and follow-up ranged from 2 days to 1 year.

sec.title: Pain scores
sec.p:
Compared to the control group, intravenous dexamethasone significantly reduced VAS pain scores both at rest (95% CI: −0.71 [−0.86, −0.55], I²=66%, P < 0.00001) and during movement (95% CI: −0.89 [−1.23, −0.55], I²=91%, P < 0.00001) 24 h post-TKA, as well as at 48 h post-TKA at rest (95% CI: −0.30 [−0.43, −0.18], I²=46%, P < 0.00001) and during movement (95% CI: −0.42 [−0.62, −0.23], I²=84%, P < 0.0001) (Figs. 3 and 4). No significant differences were observed between single and repeated dosing (P > 0.05).Fig. 3

sec.title: Cumulative morphine consumption
sec.p: Intravenous dexamethasone administration resulted in reduced cumulative morphine consumption at 24 h (95% CI: −3.06 [−4.82, −1.30] mg, I²=46%, P = 0.0006) and 48 h (95% CI: −5.23 [−8.28, −2.18] mg, I²=76%, P = 0.0008) postoperatively. Subgroup analyses showed no significant difference between single and repeated doses in cumulative morphine consumption (P > 0.05) (Fig. 5).

caption.p: Forest plot of cumulative morphine consumption within 24 h and 48 h

sec.title: Walking distance and ROM
sec.p: Data from three studies [21, 28, 30], involving 407 patients, indicated that postoperative walking distances for the dexamethasone group were significantly longer than those of the control group on postoperative day 1 (POD1) (95% CI: 6.11 [0.21, 12.01] m, I²=77%, P = 0.04), POD2 (95% CI: 7.46 [3.80, 11.12] m, I²=0%, P < 0.0001), and POD3 (95% CI: 8.51 [0.83, 16.20] m, I²=55%, P = 0.03) (Annex 2 Fig. 1). Additionally, ROM improvements were noted on POD1 (95% CI: 7.34 [1.95, 12.74], I²=73%, P = 0.008) and POD2 (95% CI: 3.20 [0.32, 6.09], I²=0%, P = 0.03), while ROM on POD3 did not significantly differ from the control group (95% CI: 1.98 [−1.33, 5.29], I²=0%, P = 0.24) (Annex 2 Fig. 2).

sec.title: Number of patients requiring rescue analgesics and antiemetics
sec.p: The requirement for rescue analgesics due to intolerable pain and for rescue antiemetics due to intolerable vomiting post-TKA was notably influenced by the perioperative use of dexamethasone. The analysis revealed a significant reduction in the number of patients requiring rescue analgesics (RR = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.16–0.35, I²=28%, P < 0.00001) and antiemetics (RR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.24–0.46, I²=42%, P < 0.00001) in the dexamethasone group compared to controls (Annex 2 Figs. 3 and 4). The difference between single and repeated dexamethasone dosing in terms of rescue analgesics was not significant (P = 0.14); however, a statistically significant difference was noted for rescue antiemetics, with repeated dosing showing greater effectiveness than single dosing (P = 0.03).

sec.title: LOS
sec.p: Patients treated with dexamethasone exhibited a statistically significant reduction in LOS compared to the control group (95% CI: −0.13 [−0.24 to −0.01], I²=0%, P = 0.03). Additionally, repeated doses of dexamethasone were significantly associated with decreased LOS (P = 0.01). Nonetheless, no significant difference was found between single-dose and repeat-dose groups regarding LOS (P = 0.14 > 0.05) (Annex 2 Fig. 5).

sec.title: C-reactive protein (CRP) and Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
sec.p: Seven studies [28–34] assessed postoperative CRP levels in TKA patients, with significant reductions observed in different postoperative days (POD1, POD2, POD3) among these studies, indicating a consistent anti-inflammatory effect of dexamethasone (P < 0.05). However, due to limited specific CRP values available, statistical analysis was not conducted. Regarding IL-6 levels, significant reductions were noted in POD1, POD2, and POD3 in five studies [28, 31–34], underscoring the consistent anti-inflammatory effect of dexamethasone (P < 0.05). Nonetheless, comprehensive statistical analysis was precluded due to limited specific IL-6 values, with only one study [28] providing detailed IL-6 data.

sec.title: Quality of recovery questionnaire (QoR) and muscle power scale
sec.p: Improvements in QoR scores on POD1 were significantly higher in the dexamethasone-treated group compared to the control group (95% CI: 1.43 [0.55–2.31], I²=50%, P = 0.001) (Annex 2 Fig. 6). Additionally, muscle power scale ratings on POD3 were significantly improved in the dexamethasone group (95% CI: 0.45 [0.24–0.65], I²=16%, P < 0.0001). However, no significant differences in muscle power scale were observed on POD1 and POD2 between the dexamethasone and control groups (P > 0.05) (Annex 2 Fig. 7).

sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p: The incidence of postoperative adverse events such as infection (RD = 0,95% CI: −0.01 to 0.01, I2 = 0%, P = 0.79), gastrointestinal hemorrhage, wound healing complications (RD = 0,95% CI: −0.01 to 0.01, I2 = 0%, P = 0.82), and deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism (RD = 0,95% CI: −0.01 to 0.01, I2 = 0%, P = 0.57) showed no significant differences between the dexamethasone and control groups. Furthermore, there were no significant differences in the incidence of these adverse events between single-dose and repeated-dose dexamethasone regimens (P > 0.05), indicating that dexamethasone dosing did not significantly impact the incidence of postoperative adverse events following TKA (Annex 2 Fig. 8).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The evolution of perioperative hyperalgesia management and multimodal analgesia for TKA has emphasized the increasing importance of optimizing postoperative pain relief, early mobility, and expedited discharge. In the majority of the studies reviewed [22–27, 29–34], a single administration of dexamethasone was given either before or after the induction of anesthesia or one hour prior to TKA surgery. Drawing from the findings of Barnes et al. [36], glucocorticoids, including dexamethasone, exert their biological effects primarily through the binding to intracellular glucocorticoid receptors and subsequent modulation of transcription protein synthesis, typically manifesting 1–2 h post-administration [37]. This supports the rationale for administering dexamethasone proximate to anesthesia induction or one hour preoperatively to ensure optimal blood concentrations as patients emerge from surgery. Our meta-analysis revealed that a single intravenous dose of dexamethasone, ranging between 8 and 16 mg administered around the time of anesthesia induction for TKA, significantly reduced postoperative VAS pain scores at both 24 and 48 h, improved early postoperative walking distances, and ROM. Notably, knee mobility on postoperative day 3 did not show a significant difference compared to the control. Additionally, intravenous dexamethasone contributed to decreased cumulative morphine consumption, fewer instances requiring rescue analgesics and antiemetics, shorten LOS, decreased CRP and IL-6 levels, and enhanced QoR and muscle power scores, without increasing adverse events post-TKA. Managing post-TKA pain is crucial not only for alleviating patient fear but also for facilitating functional recovery. Our findings are consistent with previous meta-analyses [10–14], suggesting the efficacy of intravenous dexamethasone in mitigating post-TKA pain. Recent randomized controlled trials [38, 39] also suggest that oral dexamethasone may be effective in reducing post-TKA pain, though more extensive studies are warranted to confirm these initial findings. The analgesic mechanism of glucocorticoids like dexamethasone is thought to involve the inhibition of phospholipases, thereby blocking pro-inflammatory pathways, reducing bradykinin levels in tissues, and limiting the release of neuropeptides from nerve endings, all of which contribute to reducing the systemic or local inflammatory response triggered by TKA surgery [37, 40–42]. Given dexamethasone’s long half-life (approximately 48 h), the potential for a “masking effect” may explain why additional doses within the first 24 h postoperatively do not further alleviate pain, which is consistent with our result that there was no significant difference between single and repeated doses in pain reduction post-TKA. Contrastingly, studies by Wu et al. [31] and Xu et al. [33] reported that repeated doses of dexamethasone were more effective in reducing postoperative pain scores than a single dose. This discrepancy could stem from individual metabolic differences, small sample sizes, and variability in perioperative pain management strategies. Consequently, more comprehensive, randomized controlled trials are necessary to conclusively determine whether repeated doses of dexamethasone offer superior analgesic benefits compared to a single dose post-TKA.

Morphine consumption and rescue analgesics is crucial for evaluating postoperative pain management in patients undergoing TKA. Elevated consumption suggests inadequately controlled postoperative pain. Our findings indicate that intravenous dexamethasone can significantly reduce both morphine and rescue analgesic requirements, benefiting patients by mitigating postoperative pain and minimizing opioid-related side effects. In our meta-analysis, we conducted a subgroup analysis to compare the effects of repeated versus single doses of intravenous dexamethasone on cumulative morphine consumption, finding no significant differences, which is consistent with the findings of Liang et al. [14]. Similarly, no significant differences were noted between repeated and single doses in terms of rescue analgesic usage, corroborating the findings from the same meta-analysis [14]. A limitation in our analysis was the lack of specific dosage information for rescue analgesics in the included randomized controlled trials, which primarily reported only the number of patients requiring them. Future studies should aim to document specific dosages of rescue analgesics to enhance analytical precision. Dexamethasone is renowned among surgeons for its efficacy in preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), though its exact mechanism remains unclear. It may function by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis or the release of endogenous opioids [43]. Notably, the reduction in opioid and rescue analgesic use associated with dexamethasone may also decrease the incidence of PONV. Recent studies [28, 29, 44] support dexamethasone’s significant role in managing PONV in TKA patients, a finding consistent with our analysis, which showed reduced usage of rescue antiemetics in the dexamethasone group. Interestingly, our results indicated that repeated doses of dexamethasone were more effective in reducing the need for rescue antiemetics compared to a single dose (P = 0.03), suggesting that repeated administration may be more beneficial for PONV prevention. This finding, however, contradicts the results from Xu et al. [33], who observed no significant difference in PONV prevention between single and repeated doses. The discrepancy may stem from factors such as small sample sizes, variations in surgical anesthesia, or differences in perioperative pain management strategies. Therefore, additional research is warranted to corroborate these outcomes.

Walking distance and ROM are pivotal metrics for assessing functional recovery post-TKA. Enhancements in these indices represent key objectives for orthopedic surgeons during the early postoperative phase following TKA. Van Onsem et al. [45] demonstrated that improvements in walking distance and ROM shortly after TKA are instrumental for functional recuperation and enhancing patient satisfaction. Our findings revealed that intravenous dexamethasone administration contributed to increased walking distances on postoperative days 1, 2, and 3 (POD1, POD2, and POD3) by 6.11 m, 7.46 m, and 8.51 m, respectively, and augmented the ROM on POD1 and POD2 by 7.34° and 3.2°, correspondingly, compared to controls. These results align with those of several preceding studies [21, 28, 30]. Nonetheless, our analysis indicated that the ROM benefit of intravenous dexamethasone on POD3 did not reach statistical significance when compared with the control group (P = 0.24), suggesting that the advantageous effects of dexamethasone on ROM may wane from POD3 onwards. This observation concurs with outcomes from two recent randomized controlled trials [21, 30]. The link between increased walking distance and ROM with postoperative pain alleviation after TKA underscores the potential diminution in the efficacy of dexamethasone for pain relief by POD3, which likely contributes to the lack of significant differences in ROM at this timepoint. Due to the inclusion of the randomised controlled trial study on ROM at POD3 was a single dose of dexamethasone. Therefore, we suggest that re-administration of dexamethasone at POD3 may have a better effect on the increase in ROM activity. However, because of limited number of studies that reported on walking distance and ROM in our reviewed randomized controlled trials, we were unable to ascertain whether significant differences existed between single and repeated dexamethasone doses in these outcomes. Consequently, we recommend that future studies specifically address and analyze walking distance and ROM in patients undergoing TKA, to enhance our understanding and management of postoperative recovery metrics.

When postoperative pain, wound healing, and inflammatory markers such as CRP and IL-6 are effectively managed in patients undergoing TKA, the likelihood of early discharge is significantly increased. Our research demonstrated that intravenous dexamethasone administration resulted in a reduction of LOS by 0.13 days in comparison to the control group. However, contrasting findings were presented in a recent meta-analysis by Zhuo et al. [10], which indicated that dexamethasone did not significantly shorten LOS in TKA patients (MD=−0.11, 95% CI: −0.25 to 0.02, P > 0.05). LOS is influenced by a myriad of factors including the patient′s physical status, educational background, physician preferences, and comorbidities [46]. A variation in LOS can often be attributed to a specific patient cohort, particularly when the sample size is small. For instance, a selection of patients with more severe underlying conditions or complications can inadvertently extend the LOS. In our meta-analysis, no significant difference in LOS was observed between single-dose intravenous dexamethasone and control groups (MD= −0.04, 95% CI: −0.21 to 0.13, P = 0.65 > 0.05). Conversely, a significant reduction was noted between repeated-dose dexamethasone groups and control groups (MD=−0.22, 95% CI: −0.39 to −0.05, P = 0.01 < 0.05), indicating that LOS could be shortened by 0.22 days. Subgroup analyses also revealed a statistically significant difference between single and repeated doses (MD=−0.13, 95% CI: −0.24 to −0.01, P = 0.03 < 0.05), suggesting that repeated doses of intravenous dexamethasone could be more effective in reducing LOS. However, the clinical significance of shortening LOS by merely 0.13 days remains questionable and warrants further validation through larger-scale studies. In addition, CRP and IL-6 levels serve as critical markers for assessing surgical stress, readiness for discharge, and the risk of acute postoperative infections. Our review found that intravenous dexamethasone administered perioperatively in TKA patients significantly reduced postoperative levels of CRP and IL-6, indicating its potential in mitigating inflammatory responses following surgery.

QoR and muscle power scales are critical metrics for evaluating postoperative functional recovery in patients undergoing TKA, with QoR assessed on a 0–18 scale and muscle power on a 0–5 scale. In our study, intravenous dexamethasone administration on POD1 resulted in a significant increase in QoR scores by 1.43 points compared to the control group (P = 0.001). Additionally, the dexamethasone group demonstrated an increase in muscle power scale on POD3, aligning with findings from the study by Wing Chan et al. [30]. Our analysis combined the effects of single dexamethasone doses of 8 mg and 16 mg, revealing no increase in quadriceps strength score on POD2 when compared to controls. However, Wing Chan et al. [30] indicated that a single intravenous dose of 16 mg dexamethasone more effectively enhanced quadriceps strength on POD2 than a single dose of 8mg (P = 0.005), suggesting that a 16 mg dose may be more beneficial for postoperative functional recovery during the TKA perioperative period. Moreover, our meta-analysis indicated no significant difference in muscle power scale scores on POD1 between the dexamethasone and control groups. This result diverges from that of Wing Chan et al. [30], potentially due to the limited data from only two studies, highlighting the need for additional research to confirm these findings. Despite the sparse data on QoR and muscle power scales, our findings suggest that intravenous dexamethasone administration during the TKA perioperative period may play a crucial role in improving both QoR and muscle power, although further studies are needed to substantiate these observations.

Adverse events following arthroplasty, particularly serious complications such as infection and critical conditions like deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism formation, are outcomes we earnestly strive to avoid. Although their incidence is relatively low, approximately 1% [47–49], their occurrence can be detrimental, sometimes even fatal, to the patient. Our study indicated that the perioperative use of dexamethasone in TKA did not elevate the risk of postoperative infections among patients (P = 0.79), and there was no statistically significant variation between single and repeated doses in this regard. This finding aligns with recent research by Heckmann et al. [50]and the outcomes from a large multicentre randomized controlled trial conducted by Corcoran et al. [51], which demonstrated that systemic administration of dexamethasone one month postoperatively did not escalate the risk of postoperative infections in TKA patients. Additionally, our analysis revealed that dexamethasone usage did not lead to an increased incidence of deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, or wound healing complications, with no significant disparities observed between single and repeated administrations (P > 0.05). Consequently, our findings suggest that intravenous dexamethasone administration during the perioperative period of TKA does not exacerbate the risk of adverse events.

Our current meta-analysis offers several enhancements and new insights beyond those provided in the previous study [14], thereby rendering our investigation more extensive and detailed. Notably, we expanded the sample sizes for both primary and secondary outcomes and incorporated additional outcome measures such as walking distance, ROM, levels of inflammatory markers, muscle power scale, and the incidence of deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism. Furthermore, we conducted subgroup analyses comparing cumulative morphine consumption between single and repeated doses of dexamethasone. Moreover, we determined the optimal timing for dexamethasone administration, recommending injection either before and after the induction of anesthesia for TKA or one hour prior to surgery. This meta-analysis included studies that administered intravenous dexamethasone in doses ranging from 8 to 24 mg, with the most frequently utilized dose being 10 mg. However, the inclusion of the latest randomized controlled trials [21, 23] revealed that effective dexamethasone dosages were ≥ 16 mg. Supporting this, Wing Chan et al. [30]found that 16 mg of intravenous dexamethasone significantly improved postoperative pain relief, reduced cumulative morphine consumption, enhanced muscle power, increased ROM, and overall facilitated better postoperative recovery compared to the control group and a single 8 mg dose. Based on these findings, we recommend a single intravenous dose of dexamethasone ranging from 8 to 16 mg, administered before or after induction of anesthesia or one hour prior to surgery. This suggestion extends beyond the 8–10 mg dose range recommended by the previous meta-analysis [14], aligning with the latest evidence for optimal postoperative outcomes in TKA.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study is subject to several limitations.(1) Variability in perioperative pain management strategies contributes to heterogeneity, potentially impacting the precision of our findings; (2) The role of tourniquet use and its associated effects in postoperative pain outcomes were not consistently reported across the included studies, leaving an aspect of uncertainty regarding their impact; (3) The included studies employed varied anesthesia techniques, such as general anesthesia, spinal anesthesia, combined spinal anesthesia with continuous femoral nerve block, and epidural anesthesia, contributing to heterogeneity in surgical treatment approaches; (4) There is a potential for bias due to the inclusion of some studies with lower levels of evidence, which may affect the overall conclusions; (5) The overall sample size of the included studies is relatively small, suggesting that further research with larger sample sizes is necessary to confirm and expand upon our findings.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Incorporating dexamethasone into multimodal analgesia for TKA has proven effective in reducing postoperative pain, cumulative morphine consumption, the need for rescue analgesics and antiemetics, and shorten LOS. Additionally, it facilitates increased postoperative walking distance, ROM, muscle power, and overall quality of postoperative recovery. However, based on current evidence, the superiority of repeated dexamethasone administration over a single dose remains unconfirmed. Although repeated administration showed an advantage over a single dose for the reduction of rescue antiemetic needs, the small sample sizes and varying approaches to perioperative pain management have led to significant heterogeneity, making it premature to conclude definitively the superiority of repeated dosing for rescue antiemetics. Consequently, we recommend a single intravenous dose of dexamethasone, ranging between 8 and 16 mg, administered before or after the induction of anesthesia for TKA or one hour prior to surgery, as a part of effective analgesia to significantly reduce postoperative discomfort and enhance recovery outcomes following TKA.
